prose:ch06-legal-foundations:
• A legal mandate to establish and operate the registry and to require institutions to submit data.
  • Data protection, privacy and consent, including what may be public (for example licence status) and what is restricted.
  • Data-sharing agreements between institutions and, where relevant, across borders.
prose:ch06-data-stewardship:
• Named data owners, stewards and custodians for each group of data.
  • Policies for data access, use, retention, correction and release.
  • Health workers' rights to access and correct their own record.
pers:registry-custodian:
Persona. Registry operator and data custodian

Person. Designated operational and data-stewardship team that operates the health workforce registry, enforces role-based access and audit logging, runs routine data-quality and deduplication reviews, and routes record-correction requests to the authoritative source.

Specialises the SMART Guidelines generic persona: DataManager.

Draft for working-group review Outline basis
Goals High data completeness, timeliness and accuracy; zero unauthorized disclosures; clear provenance and audit trail for every record change. 6.3, 7.2, 7.5, 12.2
Tasks Configure role-based access and tiered disclosure controls; maintain provenance and audit logs; run periodic deduplication and completeness checks; route health worker record-correction disputes to the authoritative source custodian. 6.3, 7.1, 7.2, 7.5, 12.2, 12.3
Difficulties Inconsistent identifiers across source systems; resolving duplicate candidates across cadres and employers. 1.1, 7.1, 13.3
Digital skills Technical and data-stewardship proficiency required. 6.3, 18.2
Connectivity Operates connected registry infrastructure with support for offline sync/credential verification channels. 7 (nfr), 8.3

  • Institutional capacity: permanent posts for registry operation, data management and technical support.
  • Managing dependence on suppliers and external partners, including handover and exit planning.

prose:ch07-objectives:
Chapter objectives. This chapter will help readers to:

  • Describe the core functions that any health workforce registry should provide.
  • Distinguish minimum functions from optional or advanced ones.
  • Provide a requirements catalogue that countries can adapt for specification and procurement.
prose:ch07-key-messages:
Key messages

  • The core is small: identify each worker uniquely, hold a trusted record, keep it current, and answer queries.
  • Functions can be delivered by one system or shared across several connected systems.
  • Non-functional requirements (security, availability, offline use, languages) matter as much as functions.
  • Requirements should be written so that they can be tested.
prose:ch07-identity-management:
• Assign a unique, persistent health worker identifier, linked to the national identity number where available and lawful.
  • Search, match and merge duplicate records across source systems.
  • Manage changes of name and other identity details over a career.

prose:ch07-nfr-intro: Non-functional requirements matter as much as functions. The initial set, from the chapter's key messages:
nfreq:NFR-01:
Non-functional-requirement. Security

NFR-01 Security. Health workers' personal data are protected in storage and in transit, with role-based access for people and authenticated access for systems (see Chapter 12).
nfreq:NFR-02:
Non-functional-requirement. Availability

NFR-02 Availability. Verification services are available when employers, the public and other systems need them, with agreed service levels.
nfreq:NFR-03:
Non-functional-requirement. Offline and low-connectivity use

NFR-03 Offline and low-connectivity use. Registration and verification work in low-connectivity settings, including through paper or assisted channels where needed.
nfreq:NFR-04:
Non-functional-requirement. Languages

NFR-04 Languages. The registry and its public views support the languages its users need.
nfreq:NFR-05:
Non-functional-requirement. Testable requirements

NFR-05 Testable requirements. Every requirement is written so that conformance to it can be tested.

prose:ch08-objectives:
Chapter objectives. This chapter will help readers to:

  • Explain the main architecture options for a registry in non-technical terms.
  • Help countries choose a pattern that fits their governance, existing systems and capacity.
  • Set out principles that keep the registry scalable, reusable and independent of any one product.
prose:ch08-key-messages:
Key messages

  • There is no single correct architecture. The choice depends on how authority over health worker data is distributed in the country.
  • Centralized, federated and hybrid models can all provide one consistent view of the workforce.
  • Architecture should follow governance: do not centralize technically what is decentralized legally.
  • Open standards and interfaces protect the investment whichever product is used.
